Having read this three times, my heart is filled with profound emotion. Postscript to the Calligraphic Inscription of Master Xiyuan.
This letter was written by me ten months after I had parted from my teacher. Knowing that you, a guest from afar, had come to visit, I burned incense and read it;
it was as if Ye Gong were attending at my left side. From the year Ding to the year Bing, suddenly forty years have passed.

I am startled by the ease with which time and seasons change, and moved by how the world and its times have become so different; it serves only to cause the former masters to dim their brilliance and the monastic community to grow cold.
Ji: Beholding this, it is like seeing a large jar or basin within a small vessel; how can one not be reverent? You must treasure it.
Written by Master Xiyuan at the Two Patriarchs’ National Temple for Planting Pines and Selling Firewood. "I deeply regret killing that old dhūta."
The mountains shift, yet my regrets are not worn away. My burden upon my shoulders is heavy now.

Postscript to the Recorded Sayings of Elder Chong of Dongshan.

Elder Dongshan Chong: If one practices with such rigidity, though the Way may be clearly seen, you will pointlessly take that single mani-jewel within the Tathāgatagarbha and display it atop the peak of Mount Dongshan, emitting a great radiance whose cold brilliance illuminates the heavens.
All people throughout the world will clutch their swords in suspicion, not daring to look upon it with a direct eye. Thirty years hence, someone will [coolly...]

If one examines it with the eyes fixed upon the ground, only then will its value be known; how could it be worth less than ten times the price of a city? Written on [day], [month], and [year] by [Name] as a testament.

The Venerable Ancestor Yuanzhao opened the gateway to the sea and expounded the wondrous Dharma. His tongue rolled on and on, greatly tossing the waves of the ocean of Dharma.
All the people of the world looked up with bated breath, unable to reach it; they exhausted ink upon paper, yet there was not a single word.
To say there were no words is a grave misrepresentation of our ancestor; to say there were words is likewise a grave misrepresentation of our ancestor. What does Yangyan say?
The late Master Wuzu Quanhuo’s calligraphic ink traces of a Dharma robe for the Elder Qingliang, and Master Yuanzhao’s own hand:
these were nothing more than a piece of rotten melon rind that he carelessly draped over a willow tree.
Furthermore, he offered as a gift a mantra of cursing and incantation. Had I, this little grandson, been by his side at that time, I would have needed only to give it a light tug.
A single sound from the nose: the old teacher has no place to hide his shame.
I inscribe this for the Moonlight Mountain Studio (the small pavilion at the stupa of Shou):
How magnificent! Amidst the Great Clod of Earth, there is this lump of red flesh; it has never known birth or death, following only the cycles of summer and winter.
The blazing flames constantly preach the Dharma; the wind stirs ten thousand *laṅkānaga* trees. Clearly there is not a single thing; before one’s eyes, all is green mountain.
Using illusion to contemplate my own illusion, using leisure to enjoy my own leisure. Worldly conditions naturally wax and wane; the sun and moon eternally circulate.
A Verse on the Field of Ba-Yu-Tian’s Patriarchal Ancestor:
This field of mine is situated atop the Thousand-Fathom Peak of Mount Jing. It takes the four great continents as its boundaries and the entirety of the Great Canon as its deed of sale.
The land records of the Xiangshu era cannot be obtained; the boundary markers of the Chunyou era have not been lost.

It is obtained. Yet, when one attempts to calculate its value according to the figures of the Zhizhen era, it cannot be measured. Without the need for plows or weeding, once the autumn wind arrives, the fields are lush with ripening grain;
all are like *fanyu* and *wufu*, yet among them are strung pearls and *xuanli* gems. The granaries are filled to overflowing with ten thousandfold stores.
Old Fisherman Who Catches Fish in the Snow joins his palms in joy, offering congratulations to the master of the field.
A Minor Buddhist Rite:
Opening the Sūtras (The Four Great Sections).
At the Deer Park, by the Bahudā River, that which was one unfolds into three; the spring breeze brings forth many branches and vines. A-he-he! How can they compete?
Alas, everyone! You have rolled right into a thicket of entanglements.
Gather up the essence of the *Prajñā* and the spirit of the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtras;
as for the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the waterfowl, and the forest trees—do not mistake these yellow leaves for reality.
Gold. Releasing both and gathering both together—sages and commoners alike cannot fathom it. The great trichiliocosm is gathered within the space of a single autumn hair.

When Master Yuan of Xitang raised the funeral shrine, the "Leaping Dragon Pearl" was most extraordinary; plunging directly down into the ninefold abyss, he cast his body and personally supported it atop Mount Wugong.
The moonlight is bright; a single orb of radiance, neither form nor non-form. He pats the shrine and says: "It is smashed to pieces; not even a trace remains.
The myriad fruits and the universe are all plunged into darkness."
"Xiangshangren, you have come ten thousand *li* southward carrying these bones. Thirty blows are well-deserved beneath your heels! [The Master] pats the bones and says:
"To die directly upon the occasion of the critical moment is still to see ghosts before the skull. Xiangshang Zen Master, this earthen mound will laugh at you."
The Master of Wutang’s stupa has been refined through the furnace of the sutras. Pointing to his bones, he said: "Only this single grasp remains; it is not far from where you walk.
Easy to see, yet difficult to recognize. Master Wutang, leave your cozy nest and be banished to the Land of No-Birth.
When Chan Master Chong entered his stupa, he raised his fist.
His skull was shattered to pieces; it has been several years now since it lay in disarray amidst the spring breeze. Having gathered it back, the Master remains as before.
He called to the assembly, saying, "Do you wish to see the Master of the Hermitage? Du Gu said, "The Great Peng soars through the heavens; the venomous dragon..."
While churning the sea, Zhenguan called out "Zhenguan!
twice as he applied the flame, saying: "In the past, when called, you responded; now, when called, you do not speak. Birth was originally not birth; death was originally..."
It is not death. You have clearly understood the nature of birth and death. I have one more word to instruct you:
if you wish to reach the Land of Ultimate Bliss, you must first see the youth Bingding.
It is said that the stupa of Yi Xing was moved into the Three Stupas, where his bones and finger-bones were enshrined.
"If you do not clear away the weeds of Danxia and do not transmit the robe of Old Lu, you will merely live and die in vain, sharing the same resting place as a wild grave.
Only when you enter the great furnace once more for further smelting will you finally know that the skull is originally water."—Shan.
The Sangha has opened a separate workshop for you. The Great Sangha is that upon which you rely; it is like setting up a bright mirror on a stand to reflect its brilliance.

Beneath the head seat, the fire of your lifelong mastery of calculation is present. You have already calculated the illnesses of the assembly and your own natal destiny (*mìngyuan*). How could you not calculate these?
"Concentrate! Since the incense smoke has already risen and departed, what star-spirit (xing-sha) could possibly be combined there?
This mountain monk is not naturally skilled in esoteric arts; let me turn the divination board and re-examine it. After a long silence, he said: "The Head Seat Huizhou—this is indeed this very day!"
Mars enters the natal ascendant.
Regarding the presentation of the śarīra when the śarīra of Master Wuxiang was enshrined in a stupa, it was said:
"This is the śarīra of Master Wuxiang. Thirty years ago, before Crane-Crying Peak, it illuminated the heavens..."

This "illuminating ground"—this single segment of numinous light—is not something cultivated through the precepts, concentration, or wisdom, nor is it brought about by the power of endurance or humiliation.

It dazzles the monks throughout the four quarters of the world, making them regard it as a rare treasure. As for me, this mountain monk, I am truly filled with indignation and find it utterly intolerable.
Now, fortunately, the remaining light has shone upon Donghu Lake. I simply believe that the void digs its own pit; let us once again apply profound principle.

The late Minister Chang, having manifested the Buddha-body within his coffin, appeared in the form of a high official. In governing, he relied solely upon righteousness and benevolence; weary of the mundane world, he has now returned.
In the clear dawn of spring, fresh flowers fall like rain. Such-and-such a person, having mounted the power of great vows and possessing great spiritual capacity, serves as a sage...
In his youth, he served as a great pillar and foundation stone; for the Dharma-gate, he acted as a great donor through the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

He revived the living beings of the entire commandery at a time when heaven and earth were being remade, his kindness surpassing that of parents. He raised the Sovereign of the Nine Palaces above the heights of Yao and Shun, his virtue exceeding that of Gong and Huang.

Having received one summons and then another, he was about to grasp the central axis of state power, yet the two "uprights" and the three Pengs suddenly took up residence in his vital organs. Ultimately...
"Now, where do you return? He patted the coffin and said: "The colored clouds and celestial retinue are upon the Poyang River; sail steadily westward on the lotus-leaf boat.
[This was the funeral pyre lit for] Mount Zhu’s Moon Courtyard Abbot, who died by water.

For a thousand ages, the temple atop this state has been shrouded in silence; now its renaissance depends upon such heroic talents as these. Deep in the night, the moon before the courtyard cannot be seen;
one perceives only the raging, surging waves in the midst of the stream. This person, in his youth, traveled abroad, visiting monasteries throughout the regions of Chu and Min.
Having thoroughly studied under many venerable masters, he has brushed past the profound barriers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. In his tenure as abbot, there is no trace of the axe;

in his self-discipline, he possesses the purity of ice and frost. He smiles at the Yellow Plum’s transmission to the Sixth Patriarch, grasping the oar of the fragrant boat in reverse; he intends to receive Jia Shan at Huating.
Lu Fan capsized the boat: when a bubble arises, it does not arise; when a bubble ceases, it does not cease. Striking a circle with his staff, he said:
"It illuminates and shatters thousands of myriads of mountains and rivers. How excellent! A bright pearl manifests within the fire."
By Imperial Decree the Daoist scriptures were burned;
the Han dynasty once built a high platform for this purpose. The truth and falsehood [of these texts] were personally verified once and for all.

Subsequent generations have been unable to change course, persisting instead in leaving behind wicked words to deceive the ignorant. The Sacred Dynasty is like the sun, illuminating both past and present; how could it ever tolerate what is false?
"Attained. He struck with fire, forming a circle, and said: "Behold within the Samādhi of the Firelight: the true is difficult to extinguish;
the false becomes ash.
[He then] scattered his bones at Kaikōjō.
The boundless ocean of suffering is vast and desolate. You lingering spirits and obscure souls, listen as I proclaim this:
the root of birth and death since immeasurable kalpas has not yet been severed; how truly pitiable it is! Look upon you here before me, O sons of the Buddha;

you were all virtuous and good people in former days. Some have bid farewell to their parents in their native villages; some have abandoned their wives and children in foreign lands; some have perished by the axe.
Some were struck by axes; some drowned in the Canglang River; some perished from hunger and thirst while eating or drinking;
some died frozen stiff in wind and snow; some passed away while performing royal duties; and some met with misfortune as traveling merchants. Whether noble or humble, such deaths are beyond counting.
Mournful and desolate, bleached bones fill the fields; swelling and rising, discarded vessels cover the ridges. The heavens are overcast and damp with rain;

the new ghosts harbor grievances, while the old ghosts wail in the wilds. As torches flicker in the long, dark night, when will this end? Moreover, all who hear and all who see are filled with sorrow.
The virtuous and noble ones, with one mind, gather the remains at the site where boats were constructed, and turn [the wheel of Dharma] as follows...
This wondrous scripture of the Secret [Mantra] has come forth as a bridge for your liberation. Having already passed through the fierce flames, it is now interred within the Long River.

May the Buddhas extend their compassion to ferry you across upon this vessel. To repent for the grievances and transgressions of hundreds of thousands of kalpas—turn a single thought, and that is the Western Paradise.
When Śāripūtra received the robe at Huangmei in the middle of the night, he was able to utter the "hand-to-hand" phrase before Mount Kukkuṭapāda; the *kāṣāya* was draped over his shoulder.
Elder Dongshan Chong has penetrated this to the very marrow.
The patch-robed monks have no basis to rely upon. They kick over the Flower-Treasury Ocean of East Lake;

the five thousand and forty-eight fascicles turn like jade and revolve like pearls. They overturn the old stream’s curved bench; the eighty-four thousand pores of the skin harbor accumulated resentment and deep grievance.
He then went to the summit of Mount Miaofeng, where he constructed a thatched hut. There, he reviled the Buddhas and cursed the Patriarchs;
upon a single blade of grass, he manifested a jeweled royal realm (*ratnarāja-kṣetra*). He brought forth the "Iron Dumpling of Dongshan" to choke the throats of all people under heaven.

He unleashed a great, blinding blow, committing acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) until even the Śūnyatā-deva was moved by indignation and his anger flared. He took the *...* [text ends].
Mount Mi, with a light slap, startled the boneless mud ox, rolling it into the boundless sea of birth and death.
The vast waves surge, white billows flood the heavens; once gone, there is no trace of news.
Within this state of no news, the true news is revealed. Do you all wish now to see the true news of Elder Dongshan Chong? Let go of your bones.
Go to the left side of the foot of the eastern mountain;
this praises the appearance of emerging from the mountains.
Coming thus from among the mountains of Perfect Enlightenment, his face is filled with the dust of shame.
Having never emptied the realm of sentient beings, he has merely added another calamity to the human world.
Dharma opened his mouth and struck the taboo name of the King of Liang; he took a step and overturned the Yangtze River.
Compared to such coarse conduct, there is no peer in either India or the Eastern Land.

Avalokiteśvara covered his head and entered right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Suddenly, the eyes of concentration opened. What did he realize? On the tips of the willow branches, the spring rain falls in twilight.
Sitting with knees drawn up upon the flat stone, he observes with unimpeded ears. A single handful of his ocean-like sea of compassionate heart—when will it empty the realms of all the suns?
The Cloth Bag.
At the head of Qujiang磯 (Ji), within Fenghua County, he drags along his tattered sack, wandering aimlessly and despondent, yet stubbornly claiming that his life has been one of joy;
he does not realize that the moon in the clouds is laughing at him.
Pointlessly casting off the Tuṣita Heaven, he acts wantonly and wildly at the head of the River Fenghua. Seizing the staff back, he strikes him again with force;
I wish to establish a karmic bond for our future lives.
Hanshan:
"The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are but a speck of dust. If you sweep it away from before you, it piles up behind you.
You fool! Shi-de!"
A cloud rising ten thousand fathoms high is but the dregs of a vegetable; yet to collect it into a tube and boast of it as gold—how mistaken!
When Fenggan pointed at a tiger and spoke to Lüqiu, what was he pointing at?
What words were he speaking? A poisonous heart is no worse than poisonous speech; together they compose birth and death.
A deep grievance! Old Lüqiū regrets his powerful fist;
Hanshan and Shide forget their own minds and instead point to the moon in the sky, further claiming it has nothing to compare with it—clearly speaking thus.
Two stakes; why not snap the fresh reed broom?
In the morning sun, there is not a single spot where a needle could pierce. For your sake, I shall tell you the path: at midnight, the three-legged crow flies up onto the coral tree.
Facing the moon, the white is but empty talk. To insistently say that the finger points to the moon, and then to direct one's merit accordingly—this is to fall into its reflected light and shadow.
Praising the Arhats together in a single scroll.
Moving in flocks and bands, they point east while speaking of the west; fabricating monsters and concocting the bizarre, they delude the ignorant and foolish.
Who knows their supernatural powers and wondrous functions? At Tiantai the moon is bright; at Nanyue the clouds hang low.
In praise of the painting of Fenggan, Hanshan, Shishi, and the Tiger (Liangshan):
The tiger relies on people; people rely on the tiger. When one thing is forgotten, so too are you. Each is clearly awake within their own belly;
let us gather together to awaken Muzhou. Who cares for the present or the past in the human world?
I praise Dr. Zang Tongkao: he alone is my guiding finger.
He has fashioned the profound mystery of the Great Ultimate; he regards all people in the world as mere infants, thereby curing the most incurable maladies of the gallbladder and diaphragm.
He spoke as if in jest; his features could be captured in painting or embroidery. Who, then, shall transmit this profound [portrait]?
This self-praise was requested by the Elder Chongning.
There is nothing to investigate in investigation; there is nothing to awaken to in awakening. Empty-handed, one clenches both fists, intending to overturn the broken sand-pot.
Though the gates and doors have been exhausted and one is left blind with effort, there is a measure of joy and much anger; this too has its own merit. A sweet melon grows bitter gourds.
In response to the request of Elder Hongbao for a eulogy:
He leaped out of the threefold barrier of Huanglong; he smashed through the cast-iron net of Tiantong. He measured the vast void as ten feet; he weighed Mount Sumeru at eight taels.
Relying on conditions, he took up residence wherever he was; in his dealings with others, he used only his fist and his staff.

The Master’s hand—when the opportunity arises, even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot approach it. This coarse behavior is like a blind stumble; it simply counts straight north and straight south, and there is nothing else like it.
Chongbao, you must personally realize the pivot yourself; do not learn such tricks from those fellows.
Yin’s nephew requested a eulogy for one who traveled on foot to visit the elders of the Chunyou era, whose tenure in monasteries spanned both the Southern and Northern Dynasties.

He did not maintain the "living business" of Huanglong, nor did he inherit the "archery legacy" of Taibai. Habituated to dealing with others, he would tie knots upon the bowstring; whenever his faculties were deployed crosswise, he was ever ready.
In a precarious place, he cut off the bridge. Even if one were to produce ancient texts, they would only cause the Master to smack his tongue in dismay;
he merely displays his own fabrications and proclamations, stubbornly demanding that even Bodhidharma nod in approval. He possesses no excellence whatsoever, yet excels precisely in his ineptitude.
This is the monk Yuejian, the eleventh-generation descendant of Yangqi.
In this portrait of my elder brother’s longevity, there is hair—then who is the elder?
There is no hair—then who is the younger? It speaks neither of the Way nor of Chan; it discusses neither benevolence nor righteousness.
Tranquil, they face one another as each becomes an elder. Who cares whether the two reigns passed through turmoil or peace?
Painted in colors and handed over to Sheng and Biao, it is much like planting a marker in mid-air.
The Elder Jingde Su invited a eulogy on Zen study, which is entirely free from blind ignorance.
First is the livelihood of dwelling in the mountains: with a three-foot bamboo staff, when anger arises, it whips empty space until it shatters into pieces;
when engaging in debate, it presses against the stone man until his skull cracks open. Furthermore, there is another kind of thoughtlessness...
I deliberate upon this matter: that ancient, broken sand-pot is now to be fired anew within Jingdezhen.
Counting from beginning to end, among the elders of the Great Yuan Empire, none are as formidable and relentless as you.
Chongdosa requested a eulogy;

his appearance was relaxed and leisurely, yet his temperament was exceedingly rigid and impetuous. He did not regard the Buddha-dharma as conforming to human sentiment, nor did he take compassion as a means for worldly benefit.
When dealing with people, he would shout and strike with his fist; yet amidst the snow and frost, there was the news of spring. Chong was truly his son.
On the contrary, he was filial and obedient. Seeing the axe and the shoulder-pole, he added stone after stone.

Attendant Yuan requested a verse praising him, saying: "He is like me, and I am like him; you resemble your father, and it is exactly as it should be. But at the point where they are thus identical, what is it ultimately like? A sweet melon.
Born with a bitter gourd.
At the request of Elder Chongsheng Dongyuan, I offer this eulogy:
Moss encircles the withered pine; white clouds embrace the secluded rock. His countenance is solemn and present—easy to see, yet difficult to recognize.
Linji was not yet a "white-handed thief.
Elder Lu Shan of Jianfu requested a eulogy for me:

"To the east of the Great River is not where my life-roots lie; to the west of the Great River is not where I received the scriptures. I have traveled on foot and seen the three [emperors] of the Song dynasty."
Seventeenth is the evil associate who, at the very end, crashed headlong into the "Heavenly Measure" silk net, ruining his lifelong efforts.

He regarded the Buddhas and Patriarchs as great enemies and the monks as bitter foes. Having lived in the mountains for five years, he was utterly incapable in any regard and offered no benefit to the teachings or the school;
he did not ascend the Lamp of the Dharma. He followed the example of Youfozhao in assuming the dharma seat of Xiuyan.
Lushan, you are indeed capable of bearing this great responsibility; yet in matters of the Way and its Virtue, I am deeply ashamed compared to the old monk of Wusu Guantang.
Who would waste their brush and ink to defile the Great Clarity? It is better to fish at the snow-covered piers, laughing all day long as one watches the distant mountains turn green.
The Elder of Hidden Tranquil Empty Rock requested a eulogy for Huanglong, who received the scriptures yet did not make them his home; who personally met Tian Tong yet did not transmit his way.

Born in the Shaoding era of the Song dynasty, he has passed through seventy years of the calendar; with snow filling his hair, he has resided at Jianfu in Fan for over twenty years, yet remains without achievement.

This may be examined. To use the staff and shouts as deep grievances for his disciples, and to regard his own indolence and clumsiness as the supreme treasure of the world—this is groundless concealment.
It was merely fabricated by Miaofeng; it is like a withered bridge.
Where in the far north or the far south can one find such an elder who possesses neither Chan nor the Way and is incapable of anything? Search everywhere!

Upon reading it once through, [he found that] both Buddhas and Patriarchs were all being reviled and scolded. His old resentment flared up in indignation;
instead of repaying virtue with virtue, he too uttered foul language, cursing them once as follows: "Five days after the summer retreat began in the first year of Dàdé.
